title: A Bridge Is a Promise
subtitle: A Lanternweald continuation
content:
Toph announced that the bridge was lying before breakfast.

I had not yet finished my tea.

"The bridge doesn't talk," I said.

"Neither do half the councilors until somebody agrees with them. Doesn't make them honest."

She sat cross-legged on the floor with one palm against the stone. Outside, Riverstone Terrace was waking: carts creaked over damp cobbles, someone called for fresh bread, and a metalworker in the next courtyard was hammering with the conviction that everyone else wanted to be awake.

Katara brought a bowl of rice to the table.

"Which bridge?"

"The new one. East side."

Aang looked up from the stack of meeting notes he'd been reading.

"We inspected that yesterday."

Toph gave him a look.

"You inspected the ribbon."

"I checked the supports."

"From a flying bison."

"I could see the whole span."

"Congratulations. The ground has requested a second opinion."

Katara sat down.

"What did you feel?"

Toph's joking expression slipped.

"Something moved after the rain. Not enough to collapse. Enough to stop letting people cross like it's finished."

I put down my cup.

"Then we close it."

Aang looked at the notes again. He had fought hard for the bridge. It connected a stretch of Riverstone that flooded every autumn to the higher market street. People needed it for medicine, work, school and visiting relatives. Closing it would make their lives harder.

"There's a dedication today," he said.

"Then we can dedicate ourselves to not dropping anyone in the river," Toph answered.

Katara was already standing.

"I'll speak to the clinic."

I found my boots, took the inspection ledger and followed them out.

The bridge stood between two rows of houses, its new timber bright against the darker stone supports. Someone had strung colored cloth between the railings for the ceremony. Children were chasing one another along the eastern approach while a vendor sold sweet buns beside the steps.

For a moment it looked exactly like the version the council wanted everyone to see.

Toph stepped onto the first stone and froze.

"There."

She pointed toward the base of the nearest pier.

I crouched. A thin line cut across the mortar, pale and fresh. Water had collected against a pile of debris on the upstream side, where the canal bent toward the market.

Aang looked down.

"I didn't see that."

"That's why they call it a second opinion," I said.

Katara raised a narrow ribbon of water from the canal and let it move slowly around the damaged stone. Tiny bubbles surfaced along the crack.

"The water is finding a path through it," she said. "It's not just sitting outside."

Toph nodded.

"Exactly."

Aang's expression changed.

"All right. We close it."

I wanted to hug him for saying it without making us argue first.

Then the council secretary arrived.

"You cannot close the bridge," she said. "The delegation is here. The banner is painted."

I held up the ledger.

"The mortar is separating."

"We have workers."

"We need a structural review."

"The mayor is speaking in an hour."

Toph smiled in a way that made me fear for the banner.

"Great. He can speak on the safe side."

We put the closure notice on both approaches and sent runners down the street. Katara helped an older vendor move his cart to the temporary crossing. Aang redirected pedestrians with gentle gusts of wind, avoiding the wet stones near the damaged pier. Toph worked with the bridge crew to build a temporary barrier that could not be mistaken for a suggestion.

I marked the route on a fresh map.

Then a woman carrying a basket of medicine stopped beside me.

"Your other crossing has steps," she said.

I looked at the map.

She was right.

It had been built for carts and people who could manage a steep rise. The sign said ACCESSIBLE ROUTE because someone had assumed a wide path was an easy path.

"I'll fix the sign," I said.

"That's not what I need."

I closed my mouth.

She pointed toward the higher market street.

"My father can't climb those steps. I have to get to him before his noon medicine."

"Where is he?"

She told me the address. We worked out a temporary delivery using a cart on the lower road, with two volunteers from the market helping carry the basket over a short, level section. Katara checked what could safely wait. Aang spoke with the workers about a removable ramp while Toph refused to approve a makeshift platform that could shift under a wheel.

The answer took time. It was imperfect.

It was also better than changing a word on a sign and going home.

By midday, the dedication had become a public meeting.

The council secretary had recovered enough to be furious.

"We've delayed this project three times already."

"Then let's not celebrate it as complete," I said.

Aang stood beside me, his hands tucked into his sleeves.

"The Avatar is responsible for keeping people safe," the secretary said.

"The Avatar is responsible for more than being photographed beside a bridge," Aang answered.

That silenced her.

He did not look pleased with himself. He looked tired.

The committee agreed to fund an independent review, clear the upstream debris and keep a temporary path staffed until repairs could be completed. I made them write down who would inspect the replacement supports next season.

Toph signed the review request with such aggressive strokes that the paper nearly tore.

After the meeting, I found her alone on the west bank, sitting on a low wall.

"You're sulking," I said.

"I'm thinking."

"That can look similar."

She tilted her face toward me.

"I felt it yesterday. Not as clearly. I knew something was wrong and told myself somebody else had checked it."

"Why?"

"Because everybody wanted it done. Because I wanted it done."

I sat beside her.

"You're allowed to miss things."

"Everybody keeps saying that like it's comforting."

"It's true."

"Truth can be annoying."

"I've noticed."

She reached for my hand and found it without needing to look.

"Do you think the others are mad?"

"Katara is mad at the mortar. Aang is mad at himself. I'm mad at whoever wrote accessible route on that ridiculous sign."

Toph made a sound halfway between a snort and a laugh.

"And you?"

"I'm relieved you told us."

She squeezed my hand once, hard.

That evening we returned home with mud on our boots and far too little food in the house. Aang tried to make dinner while still reading the survey notes. Katara took the papers from him and put them on a shelf.

"The bridge will not improve if you burn the rice," she said.

"That seems unfair."

"It is accurate," I told him.

Toph opened a cupboard. "Where are the bowls?"

"Same place as yesterday," Aang said.

"I know. I was asking to see if anyone remembered."

She took four bowls down, set them on the table and reached past me for the last piece of bread.

I stopped her.

"Ask."

She grinned. "You're getting predictable."

"That's what I like about me."

Katara laughed. Aang finally set down the spoon he'd been holding like a ceremonial staff.

Dinner was messy and late. We argued about costs, the council, and whether the temporary ramp should be built with timber or stone. We also talked about who needed time alone tomorrow and who could help with the supply list.

Nobody won.

Nobody had to.

When the kitchen was clean, Aang came to stand beside me at the open window. From Lanternwell Square the evening bell carried across the terrace. He slipped an arm around my waist, slowly enough that I could move away.

I didn't.

"I wanted it to be beautiful," he said.

"The bridge?"

"The whole place."

I leaned into him.

"It can be. But beauty isn't the ribbon."

He rested his forehead lightly against mine.

"I know."

Behind us, Katara asked Toph not to leave the boots in the doorway. Toph replied that the doorway had started the argument.

I closed my eyes and let the sound of them fill the house.

Tomorrow there would be another inspection, another meeting and another list of things that weren't finished.

Tonight we had four bowls, one dry floor and the right to be tired together.
